My Fair Lady. The nineteen fifty-six musical by Alan Jay Lerner, lyrics, and Frederick Loewe, music, adapted from George Bernard Shaw's Pygmalion. The story follows Henry Higgins, an arrogant linguistics professor, who makes a wager that he can transform Eliza Doolittle, a Cockney flower girl, into a refined society lady indistinguishable from a duchess, only to discover that art and science cannot account for human feeling.

Lerner wrote both the book and lyrics while Loewe composed the music in a major achievement in postwar American musical theatre, earning eight Tony Awards in nineteen fifty-seven. The unforgettable songs include "I Could Have Danced All Night," "On the Street Where You Live," "The Rain in Spain," "Wouldn't It Be Loverly?", and "Why Can't the English?" This last song establishes Higgins' obsession with linguistic precision and social order, establishing both the comedy and the conflict that drives the plot.

The musical was based directly on Shaw's nineteen thirteen play Pygmalion, which itself drew on the Greek myth. Lerner and Loewe added romantic tension and musical sophistication that Shaw deliberately withheld. The nineteen fifty-nine Academy Award for Best Picture went to the film adaptation, which starred Rex Harrison as Higgins and Audrey Hepburn as Eliza, cementing both in cultural memory.

The show ran on Broadway for twenty-seven hundred seventeen performances from nineteen fifty-six to nineteen sixty-two, the second-longest run at the time, and has been revived repeatedly since. The ending—Eliza's assertion of independence and Higgins' reluctant recognition of her as an equal—remains a subtle rejection of simple romantic resolution.
